questions.question: Describe conditions in the Warsaw Ghetto and explain what happened during the Great Deportation of 1942.
questions.expected_answer: The ghetto was sealed in November 1940 behind a wall; more than 400 000 Jews were crammed into about 3,4 square kilometres, seven or more per room, on starvation rations, and more than 80 000 died of hunger and typhus by mid-1942. People resisted by smuggling food, secret schooling and the Oyneg Shabes archive. From 22 July to September 1942 about 265 000 were deported from the Umschlagplatz to Treblinka under the lie of resettlement and murdered; Janusz Korczak went with his orphans.

questions.question: Explain why the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising took place, how it was suppressed and why it is significant.
questions.expected_answer: Knowing deportation meant death, ŻOB under Mordechaj Anielewicz and ŻZW fighters, about 700 to 1 000, resisted in January 1943 and then rose on 19 April 1943 with pistols and petrol bombs. Stroop's 2 000 troops burned the ghetto block by block; Anielewicz died at 18 Miła Street on 8 May and the Great Synagogue was blown up on 16 May. It could not win but it was the largest Jewish revolt, defended dignity, disproved Nazi claims and inspired revolts at Treblinka and Sobibór.

questions.question: Describe the main turning points that led to Germany's defeat, including South Africa's role, and state when and how the war in Europe ended.
questions.expected_answer: Stalingrad (surrender 2 February 1943) and Kursk turned the Eastern Front; El Alamein (late 1942), where South Africans fought, ended Axis power in North Africa by May 1943; the 6th SA Armoured Division fought in Italy; about 334 000 South Africans volunteered. D-Day on 6 June 1944 opened a western front; Paris was freed in August 1944. The Soviets took Berlin, Hitler killed himself on 30 April 1945 and Germany surrendered unconditionally, effective 8 May 1945 (VE Day).
